newsitem.title: USA: CalPERS adopts governance plans for Britain, France.
newsitem.headline: CalPERS adopts governance plans for Britain, France.

text.p: The California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS) has adopted corporate "governance principles" designed to improve the value of its holdings in Britain and France, a spokesman said.
"We're using this to monitor our investments, impove shareholder value, and to get these markets to focus on shareholder value," CalPERS spokesman Brad Pacheco said on Thursday.
He added that CalPERS plans to issue governance guidelines tailored for Japan and Germany in the coming months.

The British and French principles call for greater investor oversight of corporate boards, and urge boards in both countries to build on the "twin concepts of independence from management and accountability to corporate owners."

America's largest public pension fund also said governance practices in Britain and France should "strengthen management accountability to corporate owners through the director-shareholder relationship."
CalPERS, based in Sacramento, Calif., has about $3.7 billion invested in British companies and about $1.3 billion invested in France, Pacheco said.

The pension fund's board of directors and investment committee have already approved the governance principles for Britain and France, Pacheco said. He said CalPERS plans to formally unveiled them at a briefing in London next week.
In the United States, CalPERS uses its "governance principles" as one way of improving the performance of the companies it invests in.

Companies targeted by CalPERS in the U.S. have faced corporate governance fights and board shakeups. Its shareholder activism often has led to better stock performance by the targeted companies, CalPERS said.
For Britain and France, CalPERS outlined several specific guidelines.
CalPERS said shareholders in Britain have an obligation to exercise responsibilities as a corporate owner and said they should use corporate governance tools available in the British market.
The California pension fund said it supports existing codes as guidelines of best practice in British corporate governance, but added that these codes should be strengthened not weakened.
For France, CalPERS said minority shareholders should "have a right to expect" that corporate boards will represent the interests of all shareholders.
In addition, CalPERS said French corporate boards should use the Vienot committee recommendations as a minimum benchmark of their duties and obligations.
A 1995 report on corporate governance drafted by a committee chaired by Societe Generale chairman Marc Vienot recommended eliminating cross-shareholdings in French corporations.
"Toward this goal, CalPERS recommends that the Paris Bourse have as a listing requirement the disclosure of a company's complaince with the Vienot guidelines or lack thereof," CalPERS said.

CalPERS is the largest public pension system in the U.S., with more than $110 billion in assets. In addition to the state of California, it manages retirement and health plans for 2,400 local government agencies -- serving more than one million workers, retirees and their beneficiaries.
